questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i,\ i=1,\dots,m\}$ be a nonempty polyhedral set, let $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ and let $I(\boldsymbol{p})=\{i\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}=b_i\}$ be the binding index set, with $I(\boldsymbol{p})\neq\varnothing$. Which set is the normal cone $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?
options: $\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{a}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{a}_m\})$, all nonnegative combinations of every row vector
$\operatorname{span}(\{\boldsymbol{a}_i\colon i\in I(\boldsymbol{p})\})$, all real linear combinations of the binding rows
$\operatorname{Cone}(\{\boldsymbol{a}_i\colon i\in I(\boldsymbol{p})\})$, all nonnegative combinations of the binding rows
$\operatorname{Conv}(\{\boldsymbol{a}_i\colon i\in I(\boldsymbol{p})\})$, all convex combinations of the binding rows

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i,\ i=1,\dots,m\}$ be a nonempty polyhedral set and let $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ satisfy $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}<b_i$ for every $i=1,\dots,m$. What follows about the normal cone $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ and the supporting hyperplanes of $V$ through $\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, and no supporting hyperplane of $V$ passes through $\boldsymbol{p}$.
$N_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\mathbb{R}^n$, and every hyperplane through $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a supporting hyperplane of $V$.
$N_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\varnothing$, because no row of the system binds at the point $\boldsymbol{p}$.
$N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ is generated by all $\boldsymbol{a}_i$, and each row gives a supporting hyperplane through $\boldsymbol{p}$.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i,\ i=1,\dots,m\}$ with $n\geq2$ be nonempty, and let $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ be a point at which exactly one inequality binds, row $k$, with $\boldsymbol{a}_k\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which hyperplanes through $\boldsymbol{p}$ are supporting hyperplanes of $V$?
options: Every hyperplane through $\boldsymbol{p}$ whose normal $\boldsymbol{a}$ satisfies $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}_k>0$
None, since a supporting hyperplane through $\boldsymbol{p}$ needs at least two binding rows
Every hyperplane through $\boldsymbol{p}$ that contains the line $\{\boldsymbol{p}+t\boldsymbol{a}_k\colon t\in\mathbb{R}\}$
Only the hyperplane $\boldsymbol{a}_k^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=b_k$ of the binding row itself

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i,\ i=1,\dots,m\}$ be nonempty, let $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ have binding index set $I(\boldsymbol{p})$, and let $\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$. When is $\boldsymbol{p}$ a point where $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ attains its largest value on $V$?
options: Exactly when $\boldsymbol{c}=\boldsymbol{a}_i$ for some index $i\in I(\boldsymbol{p})$
Exactly when $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{a}_i\geq0$ for every index $i\in I(\boldsymbol{p})$

questions.question: For a nonempty polyhedral set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$, each nonzero $\boldsymbol{a}\in N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ gives a supporting hyperplane $H_{\boldsymbol{a}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}\}$ with $V$ on the side $\leq$. Why does this list every supporting hyperplane of $V$ through $\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: Every row of $V$ is a $\leq$-inequality, so $V$ lies on the $\leq$ side of each hyperplane through $\boldsymbol{p}$.
A hyperplane with $V$ on the side $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}$ cannot contain a point of $V$.
If $V$ is on the side $\geq$ of $H_{\boldsymbol{a}}$, then the normal $-\boldsymbol{a}$ puts it on the side $\leq$ of $H_{-\boldsymbol{a}}=H_{\boldsymbol{a}}$.
A supporting hyperplane through $\boldsymbol{p}$ always contains all of $V$, so the side does not matter.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+2x_2\leq8,\ 3x_1+x_2\leq9,\ x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,3)\in V$. Which set is the normal cone $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ at this corner point?
Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\leq5,\ x_1-x_2\leq1,\ x_2\leq4\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,3)\in V$. What is $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$, the normal cone of $V$ at $\boldsymbol{p}$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+3x_2\leq9,\ 2x_1+x_2\leq8,\ x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(3,2)$, where the first two rows bind. Which of the following lines through $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a supporting line of $V$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\leq2,\ -x_1-x_2\leq-2,\ x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0\}$, the segment from $(2,0)$ to $(0,2)$, and let $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,1)$. Which set is the normal cone $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ at this midpoint?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon x_1+x_2+x_3\leq1,\ x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0,\ x_3\geq0\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{0}$. Which vectors make up the normal cone $N_V(\boldsymbol{0})$ of $V$ at the origin?

A nonempty polyhedral set $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is described by rows $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i$, $i=1,\dots,m$. A further row $\boldsymbol{a}_0^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_0$ that holds at every point of $V$ and binds at $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$ is added, so the set is unchanged. How does the cone generated by the binding normals at $\boldsymbol{p}$ change?
options: It does not change: both descriptions give $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$, so $\boldsymbol{a}_0$ already lies in the old cone.
It becomes larger, since the extra generator $\boldsymbol{a}_0$ is added to the binding normals at $\boldsymbol{p}$.
It becomes smaller, since an extra constraint leaves fewer supporting hyperplanes through $\boldsymbol{p}$.
It can change either way, since the cone depends on how the set $V$ is written down.

questions.question: Let $V_1,V_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be polyhedral sets with a common point $\boldsymbol{p}$, and let $\boldsymbol{a}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. When does $H_{\boldsymbol{a}}=\{\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}\}$ separate them with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}$ on $V_1$ and $\geq$ on $V_2$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\colon\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i,\ i=1,\dots,m\}$, $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$, and let $\boldsymbol{d}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfy $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}\leq0$ for every binding row $i\in I(\boldsymbol{p})$, with no condition on the other rows. Why does $\boldsymbol{p}+t\boldsymbol{d}\in V$ hold for every sufficiently small $t>0$?
options: The nonbinding rows are redundant at $\boldsymbol{p}$, so dropping them does not change the set $V$.
$V$ is a closed set, so every point close enough to $\boldsymbol{p}$ also belongs to $V$.
$\boldsymbol{a}_j^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}\leq0$ also holds for the nonbinding rows $j$, as $\boldsymbol{d}$ points into $V$.
Each nonbinding row has slack $b_j-\boldsymbol{a}_j^{\top}\boldsymbol{p}>0$, which a small enough step cannot use up.

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0,\ x_1+x_2\geq2\}$, an unbounded set, and $\boldsymbol{c}=(-1,-2)$. At which point does $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=-x_1-2x_2$ attain its largest value on $V$?
options: At no point, since the set $V$ is unbounded

questions.question: Let $V_1=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1\leq1,\ x_1+2x_2\leq3\}$ and $V_2=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon2x_1+x_2\geq3,\ x_2\geq1\}$, which share the point $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,1)$. Which line through $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a separating line of $V_1$ and $V_2$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^3\colon0\leq x_i\leq1,\ i=1,2,3\}$, written as the six rows $x_i\leq1$ and $-x_i\leq0$, and let $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,1,\frac{1}{2})$. Which set is the normal cone $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$?

A polyhedral set $V$ has rows $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq b_i$; $K$ is the cone generated by the $\boldsymbol{a}_i$ of the rows binding at $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$, and $\boldsymbol{a}\notin K$. To show $\boldsymbol{a}\notin N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$, what yields $\boldsymbol{d}$ with $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}>0$ and $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}\leq0$ for binding rows?
options: $V$ is closed and convex, so a hyperplane separates the point $\boldsymbol{a}$ from the set $V$; its normal towards $\boldsymbol{a}$ is $\boldsymbol{d}$.
The binding $\boldsymbol{a}_i$ are linearly independent, so $\boldsymbol{a}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}=-1$ for the binding rows and $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}\boldsymbol{d}=1$ can be solved.
As $\boldsymbol{a}\notin N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$, some $\boldsymbol{x}\in V$ has $\boldsymbol{a}^{\top}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p})>0$, and $\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{p}$ works.
$K$ is closed and convex, so a hyperplane separates the point $\boldsymbol{a}$ from the cone $K$; its normal towards $\boldsymbol{a}$ is $\boldsymbol{d}$.

questions.question: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be open and convex, $h_1,\dots,h_N\colon D\to\mathbb{R}$ differentiable and quasi-convex, $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in D\colon h_k(\boldsymbol{x})\leq0\ \forall k\}$, $\boldsymbol{p}\in V$, and $C_{\boldsymbol{p}}$ the cone of nonnegative combinations of the gradients $\boldsymbol{\nabla}h_k(\boldsymbol{p})$ with $h_k(\boldsymbol{p})=0$. Which relation always holds?
options: $C_{\boldsymbol{p}}=N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$, since only the active constraints matter, as for linear rows
$N_V(\boldsymbol{p})\subseteq C_{\boldsymbol{p}}$, and $C_{\boldsymbol{p}}$ may contain further vectors
$C_{\boldsymbol{p}}\subseteq N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$, and the inclusion may be strict
Neither inclusion holds, as a gradient need not be a normal of $V$

questions.question: Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1+x_2\leq4,\ x_1+2x_2\leq6,\ 2x_1+x_2\leq6,\ x_1\geq0,\ x_2\geq0\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(2,2)$, where the first three rows bind. Which line through $\boldsymbol{p}$ supports $V$ and meets $V$ only in the point $\boldsymbol{p}$?

Let $V=\{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2\colon x_1\leq1,\ x_2\leq1,\ x_1+x_2\geq2\}$ and $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,1)\in V$. Which statement about $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})$ and the supporting lines of $V$ through $\boldsymbol{p}$ is correct?
options: $N_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\{\boldsymbol{a}\colon a_1\geq0,\ a_2\geq0\}$, so only lines with such normals support $V$
$N_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\mathbb{R}^2$, so every line through $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a supporting line of $V$
$N_V(\boldsymbol{p})=\{\boldsymbol{0}\}$, so no line through $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a supporting line of $V$
